families.s: HSE farm slurry-gas, pit, tanker and confined-space guidance
families.t: gas generation, ventilation, exclusion, confined-space entry, rescue, pit security, agitation and tanker maintenance
f: Slurry gases can accumulate in slatted cattle housing, poorly ventilated areas and confined spaces.
Hydrogen sulphide is highly toxic, heavier than air and may be odourless at high concentrations.
Warning signs should be displayed and people kept away during slurry agitation.
Confined-space entry should be avoided where the task can be completed from outside.
Necessary entry requires competent people, atmospheric testing, ventilation, suitable protection and emergency rescue arrangements.
COSHH assessment should include naturally occurring hazards such as slurry-pit gases.
Slurry tankers and other pressurised equipment can burst violently if unsafe or poorly maintained.
Access to tanks, pits and similar openings must be controlled to prevent falls and unauthorised entry.
families.g: Slurry risk depends on storage design, agitation, gas concentration, ventilation, weather, pit access, tanker pressure and PTO condition, competence, atmospheric testing and rescue readiness.

families.s: HSE children and public safety on farms guidance
families.t: age restrictions, supervision, machinery, vehicles, animals, slurry, stacks, grain bins and visitor protection
f: A child under 13 must not drive or ride on tractors and other self-propelled agricultural machines.
Risk assessments for workers under 18 must account for inexperience, immaturity and limited risk awareness.
Children under 16 must not operate specified high-risk harvesting, conveying, cutting, spraying or handling machinery.
Carrying a child under 13 in an agricultural vehicle cab is illegal and unsafe.
Farm machinery, animals, slurry pits, lagoons, gates, wheels, hay stacks and grain bins can attract children and create fatal risks.
Tools, equipment and access to dangerous work areas should be secured.
Unused gates and wheels should be stored flat or firmly secured against toppling.
Grain bins must be secured against entry and checked before machinery starts.
families.g: Child and public risk on farms depends on age, supervision, machinery and vehicle movement, animal access, open pits, stored materials, visitor routes, home-workplace boundaries and enforcement of restricted areas.

families.s: HSE healthcare sharps and needlestick-injury guidance
families.t: risk assessment, safer devices, handling, disposal, incident response, reporting and healthcare-specific legal duties
f: Sharps include needles, scalpels and other medical instruments capable of cutting or pricking the skin.
A sharps injury occurs when a sharp medical instrument penetrates the skin.
The healthcare Sharps Regulations require an integrated approach covering assessment, prevention, training, information, monitoring and follow-up.
The Sharps Regulations apply to employers, contractors and workers in the healthcare sector.
Work activities involving sharps should be risk assessed and exposure reduced through suitable systems and equipment.
Healthcare employers must have procedures for responding promptly to a sharps injury.
Sharps containers should be safely positioned and not left accessible to children or unauthorised people.
RIDDOR reporting depends on contamination, infection risk and the resulting injury or disease circumstances.
families.g: Sharps-injury risk depends on device and procedure, safer-device availability, recapping or passing practices, disposal location, source contamination, training, workload and speed of post-exposure response.

families.s: HSE workplace bloodborne-virus prevention and exposure-response guidance
families.t: risk assessment, exposure routes, sharps, controls, vaccination, decontamination, waste and post-exposure management
f: Bloodborne-virus guidance covers employer duties, safe work, decontamination and management of exposure incidents.
Risk assessment should identify sources of blood or body fluids and the work activities that could expose people.
Direct contact with blood or body fluids should be avoided where possible and restricted to trained people.
Contaminated sharps are a common route of occupational bloodborne-virus exposure.
Transmission risk depends on the source, viral load, exposure site and nature, and volume of material transferred.
Hepatitis B vaccination is an available control for workers whose exposure risk warrants it.
Exposure incidents require immediate first aid, reporting and prompt specialist assessment.
Some occupational infections or contaminated-sharps events are reportable under RIDDOR in specified circumstances.
families.g: BBV risk depends on virus and source status, viral load, exposure route and depth, material volume, skin or mucosal integrity, PPE, vaccination, first aid and access to post-exposure treatment.

families.s: HSE Diving at Work Regulations and approved-code guidance
families.t: project planning, contractor and supervisor duties, competence, medical fitness, team size, equipment, rescue and operation records
f: The Diving at Work Regulations 1997 and approved codes govern diving projects where a diver is at work.
Diving at work in UK waters requires appropriate commercial-diving competence for the diving method.
Divers at work require a current certificate of medical fitness issued by an HSE-approved medical examiner.
Diving projects must be planned and conducted under the applicable Approved Code of Practice.
A diving contractor must be registered where required and manage the diving project.
Each diving operation requires appropriate supervision.
Team size, equipment, communications, emergency and rescue arrangements must suit the diving technique and conditions.
Required particulars of each diving operation must be recorded and retained.
families.g: Diving risk depends on project type, depth and decompression, breathing system, water and weather, visibility, currents, contamination, team competence, medical fitness, equipment and rescue capability.

families.s: HSE quarry health-and-safety and competence guidance
families.t: quarry design, health-and-safety documents, competence, inspection, traffic, excavations, blasting, silica and public protection
f: The Quarries Regulations protect quarry workers and other people who may be affected, including neighbours and visitors.
A quarry should be designed to minimise risks to workers and the public.
The operator must prepare and maintain a quarry health-and-safety document.
People carrying out quarry duties must be competent and maintain their skills.
Quarry controls must address vehicles, edges, faces, excavations, machinery and other site-specific hazards.
Inspection and examination arrangements are required for relevant quarry areas and equipment.
Explosives and blasting activities require specialised planning and control.
Respirable crystalline silica from quarry materials can cause silicosis and lung cancer and requires exposure control and health surveillance.
families.g: Quarry risk depends on geology and face stability, excavation and edge condition, traffic, plant, blasting, dust, water, weather, public interfaces, competence and the adequacy of the quarry safety document.

families.s: HSE explosives manufacture, storage, licensing and security guidance
families.t: authorisation, effective control, licence conditions, quantities, separation distances, manufacture, records, traceability and loss reporting
f: A licence is required for most explosives-manufacturing activities under the Explosives Regulations 2014.
Manufacture includes making, assembling, disassembling, repairing, modifying, reprocessing or adapting explosive substances or articles.
The amount, location and storage period allowed depend on the explosive type and quantity.
Most explosives storage requires a licence from the appropriate licensing authority.
Separation-distance requirements can still apply to limited quantities stored under an exception.
Explosives authorisations include licences, explosives certificates and Recipient Competent Authority documents.
The licence holder must have effective control of the manufacture or storage and comply with licence conditions.
Explosives controls include security, traceability, records and reporting losses where the regulations require them.
families.g: Explosives risk depends on hazard type and compatibility, net explosive quantity, process, building and separation distances, ignition and initiation sources, security, inventory control and emergency arrangements.

families.s: HSE fireworks storage, sale and commercial-display guidance
families.t: licensing thresholds, quantities, net explosive content, safe retail storage, display duties and insurance requirements
f: HSE provides specific guidance and a risk-assessment checklist for storing and selling fireworks.
Limited quantities of hazard type 3 fireworks may be kept briefly at their intended place of use without a storage licence under specified conditions.
Larger quantities or more powerful fireworks require a licence from the relevant licensing authority.
Purchasing more than the specified quantity requires production of the applicable licence.
Safe-storage duties continue to apply even where a licensing exception is available.
Work-related firework displays must protect workers, spectators and other people near the display site.
Retail storage should control ignition sources, fire spread, stock quantity, security and emergency access.
Professional users of specified high-category pyrotechnics are subject to product-safety insurance requirements.
families.g: Firework risk depends on hazard type, net explosive content and quantity, packaging, segregation, building and fire protection, ignition sources, customer access, security, display layout and emergency planning.

families.s: HSE offshore oil-and-gas health, safety and major-accident guidance
families.t: operator, owner, employer and worker duties, safety cases, inspection, major hazards, occupational health and emergency response
f: Operators, owners and employers are responsible for controlling offshore work risks, while workers also have legal responsibilities.
Workers must cooperate with the installation manager, follow training and emergency instructions, and take reasonable care.
HSE regulates health-and-safety risks from offshore work on the UK Continental Shelf.
HSE controls offshore risks through inspection, incident investigation, safety-case assessment, enforcement, guidance and research.
Offshore safety-case legislation is intended to prevent major accidents and limit their consequences.
OMAR is the competent authority for regulation of offshore major hazards.
Offshore occupational-health management includes COSHH control of chemical exposures from common processes and tasks.
Offshore regulation also covers fire and explosion, emergency response, wells, pipelines, diving and first-aid arrangements.
families.g: Offshore risk depends on installation and process, hydrocarbons and inventories, ageing and corrosion, wells, simultaneous operations, workforce exposure, weather, evacuation, emergency response and safety-case performance.

families.s: HSE local-exhaust-ventilation design, commissioning and use guidance
families.t: source capture, suitability, commissioning, indicators, user checks, maintenance, examination, competence and documentation
f: LEV guidance covers deciding on, designing, commissioning and testing systems that control airborne contaminants.
LEV should carry harmful dust, mist, fume or gas away from the worker's breathing zone.
The system must be suitable for the process, installed correctly and used properly.
Commissioning verifies adequate control from first use and provides a benchmark for later examination and testing.
An airflow indicator or equivalent should show users that the system is operating.
Users should check LEV performance each time it is used and report abnormal noise, vibration, smell or settled dust.
LEV systems require regular maintenance and thorough examination and testing at least every 14 months unless a shorter interval applies.
Effective LEV design requires understanding the process, contaminant source, hood, duct, air mover, cleaner and system documentation.
families.g: LEV performance depends on contaminant properties, source behaviour, hood position and capture velocity, duct and fan condition, make-up air, process change, user technique, maintenance and examination results.
